lead: A map is a drawing of the ground pulled down to fit on a sheet of paper. The shrinking factor is the scale, written as the ratio of a distance on the map to the same distance on the ground. Without a scale a map is only a sketch. With one, a ruler on the sheet gives real distances in metres and kilometres. Engineers read it on topographic sheets, village plans and highway drawings, and everyone meets it on a phone map, where the bar at the corner changes as you zoom.
prereq: You need principles and classification of surveying; plane and geodetic for what a survey produces, and measurements, errors, accuracy and precision for why every measured length carries error.

sections.h3: Scale is a ratio, not a length

blocks.text: Scale compares a length on the paper with the same length on the ground. Write it as a fraction: one unit on the map stands for M units on the ground.
RF = map distance ÷ ground distance = 1 / M
blocks.where: RF is the representative fraction, a pure number; map distance is the length measured on the sheet; ground distance is the horizontal length on the ground in the same unit; M is the denominator, the number of ground units that one map unit represents.

blocks.text: These are horizontal distances. A road that climbs 100 m while running 1 km along the slope has a horizontal length of about 995 m, and 995 m is what the map shows. Plans record horizontal positions, never slope lengths.

The two lengths are in the same unit, so the units cancel and an RF carries no unit at all. A scale of 1:25,000 means 1 cm on the map is 25,000 cm on the ground, which is 250 m. It does not mean 25,000 m.

Large scale means a large fraction. 1:1,000 is larger than 1:50,000, because 1/1000 is greater than 1/50,000. A large-scale map covers a small area with much detail; a small-scale map covers a district or a state with little detail.

sections.h3: Drawing the scale on the sheet

blocks.text: A printed RF is useless to a reader holding only a divider. So a map also carries a drawn bar, built to the same ratio, which can be measured against directly.

items: Fix the RF and the longest ground distance the bar must read, say 5 km.
Length of scale = RF × that distance. For RF 1:50,000 and 5 km: 5 × 100,000 ÷ 50,000 = 10 cm.
Draw a line 10 cm long and place zero a little in from the left end.
Divide the part to the right of zero into equal major divisions; divide the single left division into 10 sub-divisions.
Label the major divisions outwards from zero and name the units.

blocks.text: That is a plain scale. It reads to one sub-division, usually a tenth of a major division.

A diagonal scale reads finer. Ten parallel lines span the height of one sub-division, and a diagonal across them splits that sub-division into ten equal parts by similar triangles. A plain scale reads 1/10 of a major division; a diagonal scale reads 1/100 of a major division, that is 1/10 of a sub-division.

A vernier scale reaches the same fineness with a short auxiliary scale drawn beside the main one. The vernier division that lines up with a main division gives the fraction directly, which saves space on a crowded sheet.

A graphical, or comparative, scale is a bar drawn for two unit systems, kilometres below and miles above, so a reader switches units without arithmetic. It also survives copying: if the sheet is photographed and shrunk, a printed RF becomes wrong, but the bar shrinks with the drawing and stays true.
A topographic sheet shows relief, drainage, transport and settlement, and its margin carries the information needed to read the body of the map.

items: Title: the sheet name and its number in the national index.
Scale: the RF together with a drawn bar.
Contour interval: the vertical step between neighbouring contours. Contours are only a layer here; reading them is taught with levelling and contouring.
Grid: reference lines printed on the sheet with ticks in the margin, so any point can be quoted as a grid reference.
North direction: true, magnetic and grid north on one diagram, with the magnetic declination for the year of the edition.
Legend, edition, year of survey, and the datum to which spot heights and benchmarks refer.

blocks.text: Sheet numbering follows a hierarchy. A large index sheet is cut into smaller sheets, each cut again, and every piece gets a letter or number, so the full code of a sheet says where in the country it lies. The margin usually lists the numbers of the adjoining sheets too.

The scale decides what the sheet can answer. A 1:1,000 plan of a campus shows a footpath; a 1:50,000 sheet shows the highway crossing the district. Flood and landslide maps are drawn on the same kind of sheet, and their worth depends on the scale being stated, because the area of the zone is scaled off the paper with a planimeter or a grid.

spec.aria: A plain scale for 1 to 25000 with a subdivided left kilometre, a divider spanning from the 1 kilometre mark to the 600 metre subdivision, reading 1.6 kilometres, and a line 14 centimetres long for a 3.5 kilometre road.

examples.question: Two points are 6.4 cm apart on a map whose representative fraction is 1:25,000. (a) Find the horizontal distance between them on the ground, in km. (b) A road is 3.5 km long on the ground. Find its length on the same map, in cm.
steps: RF = 1/25,000, so ground distance = map distance × 25,000, with both lengths in the same unit.
(b) Convert the road to centimetres first: 3.5 km = 3.5 × 100,000 = 350,000 cm.
examples.answer: (a) The points are 1.6 km apart on the ground; (b) the road is 14 cm long on the map.
examples.check:
rf = 25000
map_cm = 6.4
ground_cm = map_cm * rf
print(ground_cm / 100000)
ground_km = 3.5
map_out = ground_km * 100000 / rf
print(map_out)

traps: Writing 1 cm = 25,000 m for RF 1:25,000. It is 25,000 cm, that is 250 m; the denominator counts the same unit as the map length.
Calling 1:50,000 a large scale because 50,000 is a big number. The larger the denominator, the smaller the scale.

Using a slope length as if it were horizontal. Maps carry horizontal distances, so a slope distance measured on the ground and entered as a map length overestimates the plan length. Reduce slope to horizontal before applying the RF.

Mixing kilometres and centimetres in one line. Put both lengths in the same unit before multiplying or dividing by M; the order of converting and computing does not matter, the matching of units does.
Using the printed RF on an enlarged or reduced photocopy. The copy has a new scale, so the printed RF is now wrong; the drawn bar grew or shrank with the sheet and still reads true.

quiz.a: RF is the ratio of a distance on the map to the same horizontal distance on the ground, expressed as a fraction with numerator 1, for example 1:25,000.

quiz.q: Why does an RF have no unit?
quiz.a: Both lengths are measured in the same unit and divided, so centimetres cancel centimetres and the result is a pure number. The RF stays the same whether the map is measured in cm or inches.

quiz.q: On a 1:50,000 sheet two points are 7.2 cm apart. Find the ground distance in km.
Find the length of a plain scale for RF 1:25,000 that must read up to 4 km.
quiz.a: 4 km = 400,000 cm. Length of scale = 400,000 ÷ 25,000 = 16 cm on paper.

quiz.q: A plain scale reads a tenth of a major division and a diagonal scale a hundredth of it. Explain how the diagonal achieves this.
quiz.a: Ten parallel lines span the height of one sub-division, and a diagonal across them splits that sub-division into ten equal parts by similar triangles. A plain scale reads 1/10 of a major division; a diagonal scale reads 1/100 of a major division, that is 1/10 of a sub-division.

quiz.q: Name four items printed in the margin of a topographic sheet and state what each is for.
quiz.a: Title and sheet number for identification; scale for converting map lengths to ground lengths; contour interval for reading relief; north diagram for orientation; also legend, edition, datum and adjoining sheet numbers.

quiz.q: A planner must mark individual housing plots; a hydrologist must map a catchment of about 500 km². Which needs the larger scale, and why?
quiz.a: The planner. Plots are only metres wide, so the plan needs a large scale such as 1:500 or 1:1,000, where a 15 m plot is 1.5 to 3 cm long. The catchment is about 22 km across, which would be 22 m of paper at 1:1,000; a medium-scale topographic sheet such as 1:50,000 shows it in about 45 cm, with its drainage and contours.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital maps replace the printed bar with a dynamic one that changes as you zoom, and the true scale then depends on latitude through the map projection. Drone and satellite images quote a ground sample distance in cm per pixel instead of an RF, but it is the same ratio of image to ground. National agencies now publish open digital topographic data, and a GIS reads scale from the dataset's coordinate system rather than from a margin. Search 'representative fraction', 'ground sample distance' and 'open series maps' to go further.
